title: Choosing the Right Carrier Size for Your Dog
excerpt: A wobbly, too-small carrier is uncomfortable and an oversized one can feel unsettling. Here's how to measure your dog properly before you buy.
content:
Getting the size right matters more than almost anything else when choosing a carrier. Too small and your dog cannot turn around comfortably. Too large and they may feel less secure, since most dogs prefer a snug, den-like space.

Start by measuring your dog from nose to tail base for length, then from the floor to the top of their head or ears (whichever is taller) for height, and across their shoulders for width. Add a few centimetres to each measurement for comfortable movement, but avoid adding too much extra space.

If your dog is between sizes, we would usually suggest sizing up slightly for longer journeys and keeping it snugger for short trips, since a close fit helps many dogs feel calmer when the carrier is moving.

Weight limits matter too. Every carrier on our site lists a maximum recommended weight, and it is worth checking this even if your dog looks like they would fit by size alone, since the base and handles need to support them safely.
author: Pet Carrier Team

title: Helping a Nervous Cat Get Used to a Carrier
excerpt: Most cats associate the carrier with the vet and little else. A bit of patience beforehand can make a real difference.
content:
Cats tend to link the carrier with one thing: the vet. That association alone can make getting them inside a battle every single time. The good news is that a little groundwork between trips can change how your cat feels about it.

Leave the carrier out in a quiet corner of the house for a week or two before you need to use it, ideally with a soft blanket inside and maybe a few treats scattered near the entrance. Let your cat investigate in their own time rather than pushing them towards it.

When it is time to travel, a carrier with a top-loading opening tends to cause far less stress than one with only a front door, since you can lower your cat in gently rather than having to push them through a narrow gap.

Covering part of the carrier with a light cloth during the journey can also help, as it reduces visual stimulation and gives your cat a smaller, calmer space to settle into.

title: Flying with Your Pet: What UK Airlines Expect
excerpt: Cabin carrier rules vary a great deal between airlines. Here's what to check before you book.
content:
If you are planning to fly with a small pet, the carrier you choose matters just as much as the ticket you book. Most UK airlines that allow pets in the cabin set their own maximum carrier dimensions and combined pet-and-carrier weight limits, and these can differ quite a bit from one airline to the next.

As a general rule, look for a soft-sided carrier that can compress slightly to fit under the seat in front of you, with mesh panelling for airflow during the flight. Rigid carriers are rarely accepted in the cabin, though they may be suitable for hold travel with the right preparation.

Always confirm pet travel rules directly with your airline before booking, ideally at the time of booking rather than afterwards, since space for pets in the cabin is usually limited and allocated on a first-come basis.

We are not able to guarantee that any carrier meets a specific airline's requirements, so please check the current published guidelines for your airline before you travel.
author: Pet Carrier Team

title: Settling a Rabbit or Guinea Pig for a Short Trip
excerpt: Small pets can find travel unsettling. A few small changes to how you prepare can help them stay calmer.
content:
Rabbits and guinea pigs are creatures of routine, so any change, including travel, can be unsettling if you do not prepare a little in advance. The good news is that small adjustments can make a noticeable difference.

Line the base of the carrier with familiar bedding from their usual home, along with a small handful of hay, so the space smells reassuringly like home rather than new and unfamiliar. Avoid cleaning the carrier too thoroughly right before travel for the same reason.

Keep the journey as smooth and quiet as you reasonably can. Sudden stops, loud music or a lot of handling along the way tend to raise stress levels more than the travel itself.

For longer trips, check whether your pet may need access to water or extra ventilation, and always keep the carrier out of direct sunlight in a warm car.

title: Soft-Sided vs Hard-Shell Carriers: Which Is Right for You?
excerpt: Both styles have their place. Here's how to decide which suits your pet, your journeys and your storage space.
content:
Soft-sided and hard-shell carriers each suit different situations, and there is rarely a single right answer, only a better fit for how you actually travel.

Soft-sided carriers are lighter, fold flat for storage and tend to feel less clinical to a nervous pet, since the fabric gives slightly and the shape is less rigid. They are usually the better choice for short, everyday trips such as the vet or a quick visit to family.

Hard-shell carriers offer more protection on longer car journeys or when checked as hold luggage, since the rigid shell resists knocks that a soft carrier simply could not. They are also easier to disinfect thoroughly, which matters if you are bringing a new pet home or dealing with an unwell one.

If you are only ever making short trips nearby, a soft carrier will usually serve you well. If you travel further afield more often, it may be worth having a hard-shell option too.
